title: The Chair’s Discussion Guide
subtitle: Generative conversations for your board
intro: This guide is for Board Chairs. Use it to turn what directors learned in Governance Essentials into better conversations around your own table.

Most board time goes to two kinds of work. **Fiduciary** work asks whether we are safe, compliant and using resources well. **Strategic** work asks where we should focus. Both matter. A third kind, often called **generative** governance, asks the deeper questions: what problem are we really here to solve, what do we believe, and what are we not seeing? The idea comes from the book *Governance as Leadership* by Richard Chait, William Ryan and Barbara Taylor, and it is where boards add the most value that staff cannot.
Each session below takes 20 to 45 minutes. Use one at the start of a regular meeting, before the business agenda, or several at a retreat.

howTo.heading: How to run a generative discussion
items: **Put it first on the agenda**, not last when people are tired.
**No motions, no decisions.** Say so at the start. The goal is understanding, not a vote.
**Frame it as a question,** not a presentation. Share the scenario or prompt in the board package so people arrive having thought about it.
**Hear every voice.** Go around the table once before open discussion. Ask newer directors first, so they aren’t anchored by veterans.
**Speak last.** Your view as Chair carries weight; holding it back lets others think freely.
**Welcome discomfort.** If the conversation gets uncomfortable, it is often getting somewhere useful.
**Capture and close.** Name the themes you heard, agree on what (if anything) should come back as business, and record it.

sessions.title: After Governance Essentials: what did we learn?
sessions.when: At the first meeting after all directors complete the course.
sessions.purpose: Build a shared standard and surface the questions directors are carrying.
sessions.opener: Ask each director to name one thing from the course that confirmed how we work, and one thing that made them wonder whether we do it well.
questions: Which scenario felt most like something that could happen here?
Where do we blur governing and managing?
Is our conflict-of-interest practice as strong in reality as it is on paper?
What is one thing we should do differently starting next meeting?
sessions.tip: Expect experienced directors to be the most candid about gaps. Thank them for it.

sessions.title: Who are we really here for?
sessions.when: Before a strategic planning cycle, or once a year.
sessions.purpose: Reconnect the board with the people the organization serves, beyond the numbers.
sessions.opener: Invite a program participant, a front-line staff member or a community partner to speak for five minutes about what the organization means to them. Then thank them and let them leave before the board discusses.
questions: What did we hear that our reports never tell us?
If we disappeared tomorrow, who would notice first, and what would they lose?
Who should we be serving that we aren’t?
How would the people we serve describe our board, if they knew who we were?
sessions.tip: Resist the urge to problem-solve. Let the questions sit.

sessions.title: What would make us fail?
sessions.when: When reviewing the risk register or the budget.
sessions.purpose: Surface risks that formal reports miss, using a “pre-mortem.”
sessions.opener: Imagine it is three years from now and the organization has closed. Ask each director to write down the most likely reason, then share.
questions: Which of these risks are on our risk register? Which aren’t?
Where are we relying on one person, one funder or one system?
What early warning signs would we see, and would they reach the board?
What would we wish we had done this year?
sessions.tip: Ask directors to write before they speak. It produces more honest and varied answers.

sessions.title: When good people disagree
sessions.when: After a difficult decision, or when tension is building.
sessions.purpose: Strengthen the board’s ability to disagree well and still speak with one voice.
sessions.opener: Review the scenario of the director who posted public criticism of a board decision. Ask: what would have had to be different for that director to feel heard?
questions: How do we make room for dissent before a decision, so it doesn’t surface after?
Do people feel free to disagree with the Chair, or with long-serving directors?
How do we communicate hard decisions to members and the community?
What does “speaking with one voice” mean for us in practice?
sessions.tip: If you have had a recent hard decision, acknowledge it directly. Pretending it didn’t happen undermines the session.

sessions.title: Reconciliation in practice
sessions.when: Once a year, ideally with an Indigenous facilitator or partner invited and compensated for their time.
sessions.purpose: Move from statements to commitments the board can be accountable for.
sessions.opener: Read your current land acknowledgement aloud, if you have one. Ask: what does it commit us to?
questions: Whose territory are we on, and what do we know about the Nations and communities here?
Which First Nations, Inuit or Métis people, organizations or communities are connected to our work? Do we have real relationships with them?
What would it look like for our governance, not just our programs, to reflect reconciliation?
What is one commitment we could make this year, and how would we know we kept it?
sessions.tip: Don’t ask Indigenous directors to speak for all Indigenous peoples or to carry the board’s learning. Make it shared work.

sessions.title: The board we want to be
sessions.purpose: Turn evaluation results into a shared picture of the board’s culture and next steps.
sessions.opener: Share the top three strengths and top three gaps from the self-evaluation, without names.
questions: What surprised us?
What skills, experiences or perspectives will we need in the next three years that we don’t have now?
What is one habit we want to start, and one we want to stop?
How will we hold ourselves to it?
sessions.tip: Close by agreeing on no more than two changes. Boards that try to fix everything fix nothing.

capture.heading: Capture template
capture.intro: Record the outcome of each discussion in the minutes, or as a short note to the board.
fields: What comes back as business, who leads it, and by when
